hedges.reason: Israel's past strikes on Yemen (Hodeidah, Ras Isa, Sanaa) came as retaliation during active Houthi campaigns. In those campaigns the Houthis hit Israel and commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb together. If Israel is striking Yemen by late October, the Houthis are very likely at war again, and a successful hit on or seizure of a merchant ship by the latest rung (Oct 31) is the most direct tradable sign of that. This covers the same worlds in which my C1/C2 NO basket loses.

The listed events already show a Gulf supply crisis: a US naval blockade of Iran and Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline to the Red Sea shut since Sept 11. A renewed Houthi-Israel exchange would add Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb risk on top. That means higher war-risk premiums and threats to Yanbu-side exports and tankers, which pushes crude up. A mild upside touch of WTI in October is the market's version of the Red Sea re-tightening story.

claims.reason: Israel does not strike Yemen out of the blue. In 2024-25 every Israeli strike on Yemen answered an active Houthi campaign, and those campaigns included attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. If Israel strikes Yemen by Oct 31, the Houthis have almost certainly re-entered the war, and their main lever is merchant ships. So a successful Houthi strike on or seizure of a commercial vessel by Oct 31 should come with it.

An Israeli strike on Yemen in October would mean the Red Sea front has reopened while the Gulf is already stressed (Iran blockade, East-West pipeline shut). Tankers going through Bab el-Mandeb and Saudi Red Sea export routes would face new risk. Insurers and traders would reprice that, adding a risk premium that at least carries WTI to a mildly elevated upside level during October.
